title: OOP: Classes, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and C's Manual Approach
description: How classes, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstraction, and interfaces compare, including C's lack of built-in OOP.
objectives: Compare class/object support between Python and Java
Understand how C can approximate OOP patterns manually

content.heading: Python
content.body: Classes are defined with class, using __init__ as the constructor and self as the explicit first parameter of every instance method. Encapsulation is convention-based (_name, __name) rather than enforced. Inheritance (including multiple inheritance, resolved via a well-defined MRO) and polymorphism (duck typing — any object with the right method 'just works', regardless of its actual inheritance) are both fully supported, dynamically.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Classes are defined with class, with a constructor sharing the class name and this as the implicit current-object reference. Encapsulation is language-enforced via private/protected/public access modifiers. Inheritance is single (one parent class), with multiple interface implementation as the mechanism for multiple 'is-capable-of' relationships. Polymorphism is achieved through inheritance/interfaces plus dynamic method dispatch, resolved at runtime based on an object's actual type.

content.heading: C
content.body: C has no built-in class-based OOP whatsoever — no classes, no inheritance, no built-in polymorphism, no access modifiers in the OOP sense. Object-oriented patterns can still be approximated manually: a struct groups data (like a class's fields); functions taking that struct as their first parameter simulate methods; 'inheritance' can be approximated by embedding a base struct as the first field of a derived struct; and 'polymorphism' can be approximated using function pointers inside the struct (an informal, hand-built virtual-method-table pattern) — this is genuinely how some C codebases (including parts of the Linux kernel) implement OOP-like designs, but entirely by convention and manual discipline, with none of it enforced or checked by the language itself.

content.explanation: A function pointer stored inside the struct lets different 'kinds' of Animal have different speak() behavior — a manual, unenforced approximation of polymorphism.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python and Java both have full, language-level, enforced OOP support (classes, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation); C has none of it built in and requires deliberately hand-rolling any OOP-like pattern using structs and function pointers, with the compiler providing no help enforcing the intended design.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Choosing C for a project that heavily relies on OOP design patterns means accepting significant extra manual discipline (and losing compiler-enforced correctness for those patterns) that Python or Java would provide for free at the language level.

keyPoints: Python and Java both have full, built-in, language-enforced OOP: classes, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation
C has NO built-in class-based OOP — everything must be approximated manually with structs and function pointers
Python's OOP is dynamic (duck typing, multiple inheritance via MRO); Java's is static and stricter (single inheritance, interfaces, access modifiers)
